question.problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1,0) & =0, & \,{f}^{′}(-1,0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(-1,0) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(-2,1).$

current_example.problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,0) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(1,0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14134795/assets/7830a2af77c4965d1e7e7fd474fd8279da5b880686c17a6eceed0b5ad6f8aed4.svg) to approximate the value of $f(1,1,1).$
current_example.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $\mathbf{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is defined by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14134795/assets/dc11e717fac578e5f5c2be5446a709531123624666ac8390c548280a5eb8e9c8.svg) 

and is twice differentiable at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $\mathbf a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14134795/assets/36b3a7d98e15b0e9c3e35ea20fa38eda97513b3e71180e7de91f39ac10f7d30c.svg)

and

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14134795/assets/bfbcceebcffcbd5e6692237093f71be2c09c3399dbb3c08f4d6751b7535a7602.svg)

In this case, we have ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14134795/assets/7591b16a445c1210bd5c97468ab906ca7ddda9ad9a53b935e5bd8a4bc60103f1.svg) and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14134795/assets/4630b2a3bf15f53028807982f1f8f54f666a9b899287ce32bc890f2ce9bac56d.svg)

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14134795/assets/6cb62c6b99a268a2e2d626f7753d1e3777378343df0b05bfd6b73514da50ef93.svg) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,1) & ≈-1+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+1+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
